title: FFT Microphone Spectrum Analyzer
description: A live FFT of the computer's microphone, with a peak marker, a fading peak trail, and a hertz-plus-musical-note readout for the browser version of the whistle test.
creator: Real-Time DSP on a $5 Microcontroller
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Digital Signal Processing
Spectral Analysis
Audio Capture
chapter_title: Computing and Displaying a Real Spectrum

educational.topic: Live magnitude spectrum of real audio
learningObjectives: Apply the magnitude spectrum to real captured audio
Verify that a displayed peak tracks a changing pitch in real time
Distinguish tonal, harmonic, and noise-like sounds by their spectra
Relate the readout's step size to the FFT bin width
prerequisites: An FFT produces a magnitude per bin
Bin width equals sample rate divided by FFT size
Harmonics are integer multiples of a fundamental

controls.label: Start microphone
controls.purpose: Request microphone access and begin live analysis; toggles to stop and resume

controls.label: Demo sweep
controls.purpose: Run a synthetic whistle glide for machines with no microphone or no permission

controls.label: decibel scale
controls.purpose: Switch bar heights between linear magnitude and a -48 dB to 0 dB scale

simulationModel.modelType: Live 512-bin FFT of a microphone stream, with peak picking and note conversion
equations: peak frequency = peak bin index * bin width
assumptions: The strongest bin above a fixed threshold is the fundamental
Equal temperament with A4 = 440 Hz for the note readout
Sample rate is read from the audio context, defaulting to 44100 Hz
limitations: Peak frequency is quantized to one bin width; parabolic interpolation from Chapter 15 is deliberately omitted
The strongest bin is not always the perceived pitch for harmonically rich sounds
Microphone access requires a secure context and user permission

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Predict-then-verify with the student's own voice as the signal source
keyQuestions: Why does a hum show harmonics but a whistle does not?
Why does the reported frequency step rather than slide?
What changes when the decibel scale is switched on, and what does not?
commonMisconceptions: That the tallest bar is always the perceived pitch
That switching to a decibel scale makes the quiet content louder rather than more visible
That a wider displayed frequency range improves frequency resolution
assessmentOpportunities: Bound the true frequency given a reported peak and the bin width
Classify a recorded sound as tonal, harmonic, or noise-like from its spectrum
